query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of titanium to the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will promote the in‐situ formation of a stable, lubricious oxide layer during sliding that protects the surface and maintains low friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix with no intentional secondary phases or oxide formers.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by adding a controlled, small fraction of titanium (e.g., a few atomic percent) to the CoCrFeNi system.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests carried out in ambient air under a constant load over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine, uniform Ti-rich oxide layer (e.g., TiO2 or mixed oxides with Cr/Co) at the sliding interface, which acts as a protective, low-shear film.
generation.mechanism: Titanium, having a strong tendency to form stable and adherent oxides, will oxidize during sliding at elevated temperatures, creating a continuous, lubricious oxide scale. This oxide minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, reducing adhesive wear and friction. At lower temperatures the modification should minimally affect the primary microstructure, while at higher temperatures the protective oxide layer becomes more pronounced.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-alloyed CoCrFeNi alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate over the entire temperature range compared with the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which tends to show increased friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to the lack of a stable protective oxide layer.
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature up to 800 °C; applied sliding load typical of wear testing in ambient air; experiment conducted under controlled environmental conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti content for balancing oxide formation with other mechanical properties is not yet determined, and the stability of the oxide under cyclic sliding and thermal fluctuations is subject to further experimentation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one with the baseline CoCrFeNi composition and one with the same alloy modified by the addition of titanium. Perform controlled sliding wear tests at multiple temperatures (e.g., room temperature, 400 °C, and 800 °C) while monitoring the friction coefficient and quantifying the wear rate. In parallel, characterize the wear track surfaces using surface analysis techniques (e.g., XPS, Raman spectroscopy) to verify the formation and continuity of the Ti-rich oxide layer.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and morphology (using XPS, SEM, or Raman spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-containing alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the tested temperature range compared to the baseline, or if no stable, continuous Ti-rich oxide layer is observed at the wear surfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
